Power tariff hike puts Bangladesh’s heat protection at risk
item.description:
Rising electricity tariffs could make essential cooling increasingly unaffordable for low-income households as Bangladesh faces more frequent and intense periods of extreme heat.
The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) raised electricity tariffs in June, increasing the wholesale rate from Tk7 to Tk8.39 per kilowatt-hour, a 19.85% rise.
The weighted average retail tariff also increased by 16.68%, from Tk9.11 to Tk10.63 per unit.
BERC retained lifeline rates for low-volume consumers, however, keeping the tariff at Tk4.63 for households using less than 50 units a month and Tk5.26 for those using less than 75 units. The adjusted average retail tariff was set at Tk10.40 per unit.
The increase is more significant for households that consume more electricity for cooling.
Under the revised tariff, residential consumers using 76 to 200 units a month now pay Tk8.50 per unit for consumption above the first 75 units, up from Tk7.20.
For a household consuming 200 units a month, the electricity charge has increased from Tk1,294.50 to Tk1,457, an additional Tk162.50 before demand charges and VAT.
For low-income families already limiting electricity use because of rising living costs, the increase could make it harder to run fans and other cooling appliances for longer periods during extreme heat.
The tariff hike comes as Bangladesh's heat burden is growing, with rising temperatures posing increasing risks to public health and productivity.
A new publication by the Climate Impact Lab projects nearly 430,000 additional heat-related deaths globally every year by 2050. Poorer countries are expected to record mortality rates 10 times higher than affluent regions.
Bangladesh is among 18 countries identified as particularly vulnerable, where rapidly rising extreme heat is expected to coincide with limited growth in electricity consumption for cooling.
The researchers warn that simply connecting households to the electricity grid will not be enough. People also need to be able to afford the electricity required to cool themselves during dangerous heat episodes — what the researchers describe as a potential “mortality-cooling trap.”
Bangladesh had an electrification rate of 99.5% by 2023, according to World Bank data.
Yet access to electricity does not translate into equal access to cooling.
Affluent households can increasingly rely on air conditioners, while many low-income families have to limit even basic fan use because of electricity costs.
The disparity is particularly evident in Dhaka, where rapid urbanization, concrete surfaces, dense construction and heavy traffic have intensified heat exposure.
Between 1980 and 2023, Bangladesh's maximum temperature increased by 1.1°C, while the national heat index rose by 4.5°C.
In Dhaka, the maximum temperature increased by 1.4°C, while the rise in the heat index was roughly 65% higher than the national average.
The loss of 47% of the capital's dense green space between 1989 and 2020 has further intensified the city's vulnerability to heat.
The economic cost is also substantial.
The World Bank estimates that heat-related physical and mental illnesses caused around 250 million lost workdays in Bangladesh in 2024, resulting in an economic loss of $1.78 billion, equivalent to nearly 0.4% of GDP.
A 2024 survey of more than 16,000 people found that high temperatures were associated with heatstroke, exhaustion, chronic fatigue, respiratory illnesses, diarrhea, anxiety and depression. Women were particularly vulnerable to severe exhaustion.
Higher electricity costs could further compound these health risks by making access to cooling increasingly dependent on household income.
The Climate Impact Lab has warned that access to cooling is likely to remain deeply unequal, particularly in poorer countries where electricity consumption is expected to grow more slowly.
This could leave vulnerable populations increasingly exposed to heat-related health risks even as wealthier households are able to expand their use of air conditioning.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a broader approach to heat protection.
Its guidance calls for heat-health warning systems, heat-action plans, measures to reduce heat exposure and access to cool spaces for people who cannot adequately cool their homes.
The WHO also recommends giving particular attention to vulnerable populations during extreme heat and identifies air-conditioned public buildings as one option for people without adequate cooling at home.
The World Bank has likewise called for stronger adaptation measures in Bangladesh as heat intensifies.
Urban planning, expanded green spaces and measures to reduce people's exposure to extreme heat are among the measures it has identified as necessary.

item.title: Bangladesh among top 5 countries of asylum seekers in UK: Sarah Cook
item.description:
Bangladesh and the United Kingdom have stressed the need for joint efforts to prevent exploitation, irregular migration and human trafficking.

Both the countries also laid emphasis on developing skilled workers for the international labour market, says a press release.

The issue was discussed during a meeting between Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury and British High Commissioner to Bangladesh Sarah Cook at the minister’s office in Dhaka today, Sunday.

The minister reiterated the government’s commitment to creating skilled and quality human resources, ensuring safe and decent employment and protecting the rights, dignity and overall welfare of migrant workers.

He sought UK support for English-language, technical and vocational training to develop workers according to the demands of the British labour market.

The minister also stressed cooperation in strengthening the capacity of technical training centres and Institutes of Marine Technology, as well as developing green and digital skills.

Ariful also stressed maintaining the continuity of the RAISE project, implemented in partnership with the FCDO, ILO and World Bank for the sustainable rehabilitation and social reintegration of returnee migrants.

Ariful Haque Choudhury also proposed forming a joint working group to implement decisions from bilateral discussions and monitor migration and skills-development activities.

State Minister Md Nurul Haque said training centres in Bangladesh could be linked with UK institutions to develop internationally certified workers in line with European labour-market demands.

British High Commissioner Sarah Cook said the UK was interested in working with Bangladesh to develop skilled workers in line with international labour-market demands.

She also raised the UK’s concerns over safe, regular and affordable labour migration from Bangladesh and said cooperation would be strengthened to improve the migration system.

On irregular migration to the UK, Cook said the British government and people had adopted a strict position on asylum seekers.

She said Bangladesh was currently among the top five countries of origin of asylum seekers in the UK.

According to the high commissioner, only a small number of recent asylum applications from Bangladesh have been approved, while the rest are being deported to their respective countries.

She added that people whose asylum applications are rejected and who voluntarily return to their home countries are offered £3,000 in financial assistance for rehabilitation. However, the assistance is not available to those who are deported through legal procedures.

Officials from the British High Commission and the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment were also present at the meeting.

Survey: Police struggle for public trust as Army tops approval ratings
item.description:
The Bangladesh Army enjoys by far the strongest public approval among major national institutions, while police are the only institution surveyed where disapproval outweighs approval, according to the latest International Republican Institute (IRI) survey.
The findings reveal a sharp contrast in how Bangladeshis perceive different state and social institutions, with the Army receiving an approval rating of 78%.
The High Court and local government institutions, upazila parishads and city corporations, follow with approval ratings of around 61% each.
The media receives about 59% approval, while religious leaders stand at around 58%.
Public assessments become less positive further down the institutional rankings.
The student movement receives an approval rating of about 56%, while the Election Commission stands at roughly 53%.
Political parties collectively fare worse, receiving around 51% approval.
Police sit at the bottom of the list.
Only 45% approve of the job police are doing, while 52% disapprove, making police the only institution covered by the question with a negative net approval rating.
The findings are significant as Bangladesh continues to debate institutional reform and public confidence in state agencies following the political upheaval of 2024 and the February 2026 national election.
IRI asked respondents whether they strongly or somewhat approved or disapproved of the performance of nine institutions and groups: the Army, High Court, local government bodies, media, religious leaders, student movement, Election Commission, political parties and police.
The results suggest that public confidence varies substantially across institutions, with security institutions themselves receiving sharply different assessments.
The nationwide survey was conducted among 5,000 voting-age adults between May 16 and June 24, with a margin of error of ±1.7 percentage points.

item.title: IRI survey: Bangladesh almost evenly split over country’s direction
item.description:
Bangladeshis are almost evenly divided over whether the country is moving in the right direction, with public optimism declining since late last year, according to the latest International Republican Institute (IRI) survey.
The nationwide poll found that 46% of respondents believe Bangladesh is heading in the right direction, while 44% think it is moving in the wrong direction. Another 9% did not know or declined to answer.
The narrow two-point gap marks a significant shift from October 2025, when 53% believed the country was heading in the right direction and 42% said the opposite.
The findings suggest that the optimism recorded last year has weakened as Bangladesh navigates its post-election political and economic transition.
The mood also varies considerably across the country.
Rangpur emerged as the most optimistic division, with 59% saying Bangladesh was heading in the right direction. Barisal followed at 52% and Chittagong at 51%.
At the other end, only 29% of respondents in Sylhet said the country was moving in the right direction, while 59% said it was heading the wrong way.
Dhaka was also more pessimistic than optimistic, with 42% saying right direction against 48% saying wrong direction.
Among those who said Bangladesh was heading in the wrong direction, the most frequently cited reason was rising commodity prices, mentioned by 18%.
Another 17% pointed to deterioration in law and order and the judicial situation, while 10% cited increasing corruption.
Gas shortages, lack of employment opportunities and low agricultural prices were among the other concerns.
The findings show that the public verdict on the country’s overall trajectory remains finely balanced despite comparatively positive assessments of democracy recorded elsewhere in the same survey.
IRI surveyed 5,000 adults across all 64 districts between May 16 and June 24.

item.title: IRI survey: BNP gains public favour as Jamaat loses ground
item.description:
Public attitudes towards Bangladesh’s major political parties have shifted since last year, with the BNP gaining favour while Jamaat-e-Islami has lost ground, according to the latest nationwide survey by the International Republican Institute (IRI).
The June 2026 survey shows that 57% of respondents hold a favourable view of the BNP, up from 51% in October 2025.
The increase gives the party the highest favourability among the major political forces measured in the survey.
Jamaat-e-Islami, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. Its favourability fell to 48%, down from 53% in October last year.
The findings point to a changing political landscape following the February 2026 national parliamentary election.
The National Citizen Party (NCP), which emerged from the political realignment following the July 2024 uprising, remains further behind the two established parties.
Its favourability stands at around 37%, little changed from the previous survey.
The Awami League continues to face the most difficult public perception among the major parties surveyed.
Only around 22% of respondents expressed favourable views of the party, while roughly 72% viewed it unfavourably.
IRI asked respondents whether they strongly or somewhat liked or disliked nine political parties, including the BNP, Jamaat, NCP, Islami Andolan Bangladesh, Awami League and Jatiya Party.
The latest findings are particularly significant because they capture public attitudes several months after the February election, providing an early indication of how the country’s political forces are being perceived in the post-election environment.
The survey was conducted between May 16 and June 24 among 5,000 adults across all 64 districts. IRI said the nationally representative survey has a margin of error of ±1.7 percentage points.

item.title: Foreign minister at briefing: Dhaka seeks enabling environment to advance Bangladesh–India ties
item.description:
Bangladesh has urged India to help create a conducive environment for advancing relations between the two neighbouring countries. The message was conveyed during Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi’s first courtesy meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday morning.

Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman disclosed the matter to journalists at a briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the afternoon, following the meeting at the prime minister’s secretariat.

He said emphasis had been placed on creating the kind of “enabling environment” necessary to take bilateral relations forward.

The foreign minister said Bangladesh had also urged New Delhi to expedite the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been sentenced to death for crimes against humanity, and is currently in India.

Dhaka also requested the extradition of those suspected of murdering Inqilab Moncho convenor Shaheed Sharif Osman Bin Hadi, he added.

Referring to reports that Hadi’s suspected killers had been apprehended in India, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have provided them with all the documents they requested. This is an extremely sensitive issue for us [the Hadi case]. We have asked them to extradite the killers to us as soon as possible.”

Asked whether the issues of border killings and push-ins had been discussed during the meeting, the foreign minister said they had, albeit briefly.

“These are not matters for discussion at the prime ministerial level,” he said, adding that the issues had been discussed during his meeting with the Indian high commissioner yesterday, Sunday.

Asked whether Bangladesh’s earlier expression of displeasure to India over the events of 5 August had come up in Monday’s discussion, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have clearly stated our position regarding 5 August, and the Indian authorities have taken it seriously. They told me this yesterday, and they told the prime minister the same thing today.”

There will be issues, and they will be resolved: Dinesh Trivedi

Asked whether India had expressed regret over allowing Sheikh Hasina to address a press conference in New Delhi on 5 August, the second anniversary of the July uprising, the foreign minister said the matter should not be framed simply in terms of an apology.

“You have to understand clearly what happened,” he said. “A state has three branches—the executive, the legislature and the judiciary. Convicted Hasina belongs to the jurisdiction of the judiciary. A court in Bangladesh tried her and sentenced her. What happens in the case of a convicted person? They are taken into custody, and if they have anything to say in their defence, they say it before the court.”

Elaborating on the matter, Khalilur Rahman said, “What Hasina did on 5 August was to spread hatred against Bangladesh’s judiciary—one of the three branches of the state—and the Indian government allowed her to do so.”

He added, “As I said yesterday, we want every country to respect the entire constitutional structure of our state. We hope the Indian government will understand and appreciate this, and I believe they have understood the matter. We hope they will not do anything further that undermines any branch of our state. Based on my discussions with them, I am somewhat reassured, and I hope there will be no recurrence of such an incident.”

Dhaka asks Delhi to expedite Hasina extradition, return Hadi killers

Asked whether the Bangladesh government had accepted an invitation for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit New Delhi after India extended invitations to him on two occasions, the foreign minister said, “First of all, I am not a fortune-teller. Secondly, the prime minister was not invited to BRICS. He was invited as the chair of BIMSTEC. You should try to understand that distinction.”

He further said that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had previously sent a letter to Bangladesh’s prime minister, which was handed over on the day the new government was formed. “There is an invitation,” he said.

Asked in a follow-up question whether the invitation to visit Delhi had been discussed when the Indian high commissioner met the prime minister on Monday, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have not yet taken any decision on this.”

item.title: Record July heat in regions home to 900m people
item.description:
Regions home to around 900 million people experienced their hottest July on record in 2026, including in the Sahel, Central America, France and Spain, according to AFP analysis of Copernicus data.
Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.
Some countries with well-resourced national weather agencies, including France and Spain, independently confirmed record-breaking conditions through analyses by Meteo-France and Spain’s Aemet meteorological service.
However, many lower-income countries do not publish detailed climate data.
AFP therefore complemented the global picture by independently analyzing data from the European Copernicus program.
The dataset combines observations from satellites operated by multiple countries, weather stations on land, at sea and in the air, together with climate modelling. It provides hourly global coverage dating back to 1970.
Nearly 400 million of the roughly 900 million people residing in affected areas live in Africa, primarily within the Sahel region.
Ten countries in the semi-arid belt across western and northern Africa broke their monthly heat records for July, including Mauritania, Niger and Burkina Faso.
In eastern Africa, Sudan, Kenya and Ethiopia also broke records.
Temperature variations and anomalies in countries close to the equator are typically smaller than in temperate climates.
Yet countries such as Chad and Sudan recorded July temperatures more than 2°C above the 1981-2010 average.
Episodes of extreme heat have become almost 10 times more likely since 2015, scientists from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) network warned in January, attributing the rise to human-driven climate change.
Sahel countries are among the most vulnerable to rising temperatures, while many are already grappling with armed conflict, food insecurity and widespread poverty.
The naturally-occurring El Nino climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across Central America and northern South America.
From Mexico to northern Brazil, stretching from the Pacific coast to the Guiana Highlands, approximately 110 million people experienced their hottest July on record.
El Salvador, Nicaragua and Honduras, located in the so-called “Dry Corridor,” all set monthly temperature records in both June and July, heightening concerns over famine.
The United Nations World Food Program (WFP) said last week that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.
Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.
Nearly 120 million Europeans live in regions where July 2026 was the hottest ever recorded.
The records were concentrated in southern Britain, western France, and northern and eastern Spain.
In France, average temperatures were 3.8°C above the 1991-2020 normal -- a reference period already significantly warmer than the pre-industrial climate of 1850-1900.
France and Spain also registered record levels of drought, which fueled devastating wildfires.
A megafire burned nearly 42,000 hectares and forced the evacuation of more than 220,000 people in France’s Gironde department in late July.
At the same time, Spain’s largest wildfire in recent history scorched almost 44,000 hectares in Avila province, near Madrid.
Other smaller and more scattered regions, home to a combined population of over 250 million, also experienced unprecedented July heat, including China’s Sichuan province, US states Wyoming and Colorado and the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo.

item.title: Nearly 7 lakh fail as SSC pass rate hits 19-year low
item.description:
Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examinations have delivered one of the starkest warnings yet about the state of secondary education, with nearly four in every 10 candidates failing this year as the national pass rate plunged to 62.25%, its lowest level since 2007.
The decline is not confined to the headline pass rate.
GPA-5 achievements have fallen sharply, the number of institutions where every candidate failed has more than doubled, boys are trailing girls by a wide margin, and humanities students have emerged as particularly vulnerable.
The results have brought longstanding weaknesses in English and mathematics, teacher shortages, classroom learning and curriculum implementation back into focus, raising a larger question over whether years of relatively high pass rates had masked deeper learning deficiencies.
Of the 1,829,485 candidates who appeared in the SSC and equivalent examinations this year, 1,138,897 passed and 690,608 failed.
The pass rate fell 6.20 percentage points from 68.45% in 2025.
The number of GPA-5 achievers also dropped by 22,356, from 139,032 last year to 116,676 this year.
The last time the national pass rate was lower was in 2007, when 58.36% of candidates passed.
From 93% to 62% in five years
The scale of the decline becomes more striking against Bangladesh’s recent examination history.
After standing at 72.18% in 2008, the pass rate crossed 80% in 2011 and remained above that level for seven consecutive years. It peaked at 91.34% in 2014.
The Covid-affected examination of 2021, conducted with fewer subjects and a shortened syllabus, produced an exceptional 93.58% pass rate.
Since then, the trajectory has largely been downward, 87.44% in 2022 and 80.39% in 2023, before a temporary rise to 83.04% in 2024.
With full marks and the full syllabus returning, the rate plunged to 68.45% in 2025 and has now fallen further to 62.25%.
The two consecutive years of steep decline have strengthened concerns that the problem goes beyond tougher examinations or stricter evaluation.
English and mathematics have emerged as major pressure points, particularly for humanities students.
Prof Syed Akhtaruzzaman, chairman of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and Dhaka Education Board, said humanities students performed particularly poorly in the two subjects, while science students did relatively better.
The results show the scale of the problem.
Among male humanities candidates under the nine general education boards, only 41.14% passed.
The rate among female humanities candidates was 54.38%.
The recurring weakness in English and mathematics raises questions over why learning gaps in two fundamental subjects are not being identified and addressed before students reach the SSC examination.
Teacher shortages could be another part of the problem.
Parents have complained that some schools are operating with substantially fewer teachers than required, leaving students increasingly dependent on private tuition, coaching or their own resources.
Educationist Dr Siddiqur Rahman Khan pointed to broader weaknesses in curriculum implementation, teacher training, remuneration and benefits, questioning how such large numbers could fail after completing school-level selection examinations and receiving additional preparation time.
Perhaps the strongest institutional warning comes from schools where not a single candidate passed.
Across the nine general education boards, 312 institutions recorded a zero pass rate, up from 134 last year, an increase of nearly 133%.
At the other end, the number of institutions achieving a 100% pass rate fell from 984 to 669.
The figures raise questions that go well beyond individual student performance.
When every candidate from an institution fails, educationists say issues such as teacher availability, attendance, school management, academic supervision and students’ socio-economic circumstances require scrutiny.
Where students studied also appears to have made a considerable difference.
Dhaka topped the nine general boards with a 71.63% pass rate, while Mymensingh finished at the bottom with 57.39%.
Jessore recorded 66.27%, Comilla 65.42%, Rajshahi 63.67%, Barisal 60.35%, Chittagong 59.48%, Sylhet 58.33% and Dinajpur 58.05%.
The Madrasa Education Board recorded a pass rate of 55.49%, while the Technical Education Board stood at 58.20%.
The disparities add another dimension to the challenge: whether students across Bangladesh have comparable access to teachers, learning environments and academic support.
Educationists attributed the sharp fall in SSC results to a combination of unresolved Covid-era learning losses, instability in educational institutions following the 2024 movement, teacher shortages, curriculum changes and stricter evaluation.
Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said: “It would not be right to call it a disaster, because this may be the real picture. We could not recover from the setback caused by Covid.”
She also pointed to prolonged instability and a shortage of skilled, subject-based teachers, particularly outside major cities.
Education researcher KM Enamul Haque said stricter evaluation may have contributed to the decline, but identified pandemic-era learning loss as a deeper problem.
Enamul said: “The students sitting for the examination now entered Class VI, or the secondary level, in 2020. They entered secondary education with a major learning deficit from primary school and have carried that gap with them. This year’s results are strong evidence of that.”
Md Rahmat Ullah, former principal of Kishloy Girls’ School and College, also cited stricter evaluation, curriculum changes and prolonged disruption.
Rahmat said: “Students also went through a prolonged period of unrest when they could not concentrate properly on their studies.”
Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, however, rejected the characterisation of the results as a disaster.
He described the result as not bad but “beautiful”, defending evaluation based on what students actually wrote in their answer scripts.
Students dissatisfied with their results, he said, have the opportunity to seek re-evaluation.
But the scale and breadth of this year’s decline leave questions that re-evaluation alone cannot answer.
The 690,608 failures, 312 zero-pass institutions, widening gender disparity and persistent weakness in fundamental subjects provide policymakers with multiple indicators requiring deeper investigation.
Restoring an 80% or 90% pass rate, educationists caution, should not itself become the objective. Easier examinations or more generous marking could improve the statistics without improving learning.
Instead, the results provide an opportunity to examine what students actually know, where they begin falling behind, whether schools have enough qualified teachers and why weaknesses in fundamental subjects remain unresolved until the end of secondary education.
The most consequential number in this year’s SSC results may therefore not be 62.25%.
It is the 690,608 students who reached the end of secondary education but could not cross its principal public examination, a figure that turns a poor examination result into a warning for the education system itself.

item.title: Factory fire kills 16 Bangladeshis in Saudi capital
item.description:
RIYADH: Bangladesh’s foreign ministry said it was in “deep shock” on Monday after reporting that 16 of the country’s citizens died in a factory fire in Saudi Arabia the day before.

It reported “the tragic deaths of 16 Bangladeshi nationals in a fire at a sofa manufacturing factory in Riyadh” in a statement.

The fire broke out on Sunday at a manufacturing facility in the industrial area of the Al Shifa district in Riyadh, according to the Bangladesh embassy in Riyadh.

“There were no injuries reported; all those affected died,” the embassy said in a statement.

Dhaka’s minister for expatriate welfare, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, said that there was “constant communication” with local authorities through the Bangladeshi embassy in Saudi Arabia.

“Officials have been instructed to ensure the speedy repatriation of the bodies of the deceased expatriates and to secure all necessary government assistance and compensation for their families,” he added.

The Bangladeshi embassy in Riyadh later said it remained in contact with the families of the deceased and was “coordinating with Saudi authorities on victim identification and repatriation formalities”.

Around seven million Bangladeshis work overseas — the majority in the Middle East.

The civil defence agency in the Saudi capital said it had extinguished a fire at an unlicensed facility where furniture was upholstered, without providing details of any casualties.

“The necessary regulatory procedures were subsequently completed regarding the site,” it said in a statement on X.

Like many Gulf nations, Saudi Arabia relies on vast numbers of labourers from the subcontinent to help bolster its workforce, especially for jobs involving manual labour. Reports in Saudi media estimate that over three million Bangladeshi nationals reside in the kingdom.

Foreign workers in Saudi Arabia do everything from management to cleaning the streets and waiting on tables, in a society where many citizens are reluctant to take jobs they consider menial.

item.title: Coal dominates Bangladesh’s top imports, clinker at second position
item.description:
Around 5,700 categories of goods are imported into Bangladesh each year. The list includes industrial raw materials, fuel, consumer goods and various materials used in development projects.

However, imports of only a handful of these thousands of products account for a huge volume. Some products are imported in quantities exceeding tens of millions of tonnes a year.

An analysis of data from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and its field offices shows that a total of 158.6 million tonnes of goods were imported through the country’s 46 customs stations in the recently concluded 2025–26 financial year.

The top 10 products accounted for 99.8 million tonnes. In other words, nearly 63kg of every 100kg of imported goods came from these 10 products.

Industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction dominate the top 10. Among food grains, only wheat made the list.

LNG: 13-year import deal secured with one US firm

Clinker loses top spot after 25 years

According to NBR data, clinker—the main raw material used to make cement—was the country’s largest imported product by volume for 25 consecutive years, from the 2000–01 to 2024–25 financial year. That long-standing dominance has now come to an end.

Coal displaced clinker to become the country’s largest imported product in the 2025–26 financial year. Bangladesh imported 20.7 million tonnes of coal during the year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products.

The rise in coal imports is not unexpected. Demand for coal has increased rapidly for power generation since coal-fired power plants began operating in the country. Six coal-fired power plants accounted for around 75 per cent of total coal imports last financial year.

As a result, coal, once used mainly as fuel and a raw material in industrial factories, has now become the country’s largest imported product by volume.

Clinker second, slag fourth

Clinker, a raw material used in cement production, has dropped to second place after losing its long-held position at the top. The country imported 19.2 million tonnes of clinker in the last financial year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products. After clinker, another cement raw material, slag, ranks fourth. The country imported 8.3 million tonnes of slag in the last financial year.

Limestone, which ranks sixth, accounted for nearly 6 million tonnes of imports. And, Fly ash, or ash, ranks 10th, with imports of around 5 million tonnes.

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

In total, nearly 38.5 million tonnes of the four types of cement raw materials were imported. In other words, cement industry raw materials account for a substantial share of the total volume of the top 10 imported products.

Crushed stone ranks third

Crushed stone ranks third by import volume. Bangladesh imported 16.8 million tonnes of crushed stone in the last financial year. The stone is used in the construction of roads, buildings and various other infrastructure projects.

Alongside crushed stone, large quantities of boulder stone are also imported. The country imported 5.5 million tonnes of boulder stone in 2025-26 financial year, placing it eighth by volume. Boulder stone is used in river management and various development projects.

Wheat the only consumer product in top 10

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

Approximately 15 per cent of the country’s demand for wheat is met by domestic production. The remaining 85 per cent or so is met through imports. As a result, wheat is the country’s largest imported food grain by volume.

Amirul Haque, president, Chattogram ChamberMost of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction. Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will increase as economic activity and investment grow.

Scrap, the raw material for rebar, ranks seventh

Scrap metal, or old iron and iron pieces, the main raw material used to make rebar, ranks seventh. Bangladesh imported around 5.7 million tonnes of scrap in the last financial year. The country’s steel mills melt the scrap to produce billets, which are then used to manufacture rebar and other steel products.

LNG ranks ninth

Liquefied natural gas (LNG), imported to meet fuel demand, ranks ninth. The country imported around 5.1 million tonnes of LNG in the last financial year.

Bangladesh has been importing LNG for several years to make up for shortages in domestic gas supplies. Imported LNG is converted back into gas and supplied to the national grid.

Overall, the top 10 imported products are dominated by fuels such as coal and LNG, raw materials for the cement and steel industries, and materials used in infrastructure construction. Wheat is the only food product on the list.

This means that, by volume, a large share of Bangladesh’s imports is not directly intended for consumption but is used for power generation, industrial production and infrastructure development.

Asked for his views, Amirul Haque, an entrepreneur in the cement and consumer goods sectors and president of the Chattogram Chamber, told Prothom Alo, “Most of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction.”

“Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will also increase as economic activity and investment grow,” he added.

item.title: Ukraine says Russia fired N Korean missiles in deadly attack
item.description:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least nine people overnight and wounded dozens, Kyiv said Tuesday, accusing Moscow of launching North Korean missiles in the raid.
The allegation comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned -- without providing evidence -- that Moscow was receiving more ballistic projectiles and troops from its ally Pyongyang.
Russia has turned to North Korea for support throughout its four-and-a-half-year invasion.
Earlier in the war, Pyongyang dispatched thousands of troops to help Russia fight back a Ukrainian counterattack into its western Kursk region.
And intelligence from the West, Kyiv and Seoul, has long accused North Korea of supplying weapons to Russia.
The southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia was worst hit in Russia’s latest overnight barrage, with six people killed and 19 wounded, Zelensky said.
“The city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs. It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure,” he said.
Three more were killed by Russian drones and missiles in the neighboring Dnipropetrovsk region, the local military administration said.
In the capital Kyiv, Zelensky said an infectious diseases hospital was hit, while strikes on the frontlines cities of Kherson and Kharkiv caused power outages.
A children’s hospital in Kyiv was also hit, the health ministry said, posting photos of broken windows and debris in a courtyard.
“Children and medical staff were not harmed, as they were in a shelter at the time of the attack,” the ministry said.
Russia’s defense ministry said its forces “delivered a group strike with high-precision ground-based weapons, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport-logistics centers in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia.”
Zelensky has recently renewed his warnings of deepening military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang, while appealing for more Western air-defense supplies.
On Monday, he said that Russia received “additional ballistic missiles from North Korea.”
Over the weekend, he alleged “a decision has been made for 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on the territory of Russia.”
Kyiv has not explained how it obtained the figures and did not provide a timeframe for the deployment.
But Zelensky is urging allies in the Asia-Pacific to supply air defense to Kyiv in order to counter Pyongyang’s capabilities.
Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defense pact in 2024, ahead of Pyongyang sending troops to help push Ukrainian forces out of Russia’s Kursk region.
In recent weeks, Russia has considerably stepped up strikes with ballistic missiles -- a fast and powerful weapon that is hard to intercept.
Dozens have been killed in Kyiv in the attacks.
Only the most advanced air defense, such as the US-made Patriot system, is capable of intercepting them.
Ukraine has been reporting an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors since the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February.
Kyiv has also boosted its own long-range drone strikes against Russia, hitting oil infrastructure and e-commerce warehouses in counterattacks it says are justified and designed to crimp Moscow’s logistics and revenue sources.
The latest spiral of escalation has brought the civilian death toll in Ukraine to the highest since the war’s first months in 2022, according to the United Nations.

item.title: Joblessness, skills gap, digital addiction challenge Bangladesh’s youth
item.description:
“Degrees, but no jobs”; “skills, but no opportunities”; “dreams, but no proper guidance”—these concerns reflect the reality faced by many young people in Bangladesh, according to a nationwide youth survey.
Unemployment, skills gaps, mental stress, digital addiction, online gambling and drug abuse, along with limited youth participation in policymaking, have emerged as major concerns among the country’s young people.
The survey, titled “Problems of Youth in Bangladesh and Possible Solutions,” was jointly conducted by Shopnopuri Kallyan Sangstha and Bangladesh Co-Creation to mark International Youth Day 2026.
Students, youth organizers, volunteers, social and development workers, and representatives of youth initiatives from different parts of the country participated in the survey.
An analysis of the responses shows a common reality: young people have considerable potential but lack adequate opportunities, skills, guidance and platforms to realize it.
Unemployment remains a major concern
Many respondents identified unemployment as one of the biggest challenges facing young people.
Abu Huraira Sheikh, a member of FFCRJ, and Md Mahibullah, general secretary of Nobojagoron Chhatra Sangha, said many young people struggle to find suitable employment even after completing their education.
They said the problem is not simply a shortage of jobs but also a significant mismatch between labor market demands and the skills and preparation of young jobseekers.
As a result, many educated young people remain unemployed or underemployed for extended periods.
Degrees without adequate skills
Many respondents said Bangladesh’s education system remains largely examination- and certificate-oriented.
Kaunik Debnath, director of programs and operations at Ancora, said many young people hold multiple academic certificates but lack adequate communication skills, technological knowledge, problem-solving abilities and workplace presentation skills.
Tanjela Akter Ema, volunteer coordinator at Bengal Peace Foundation, identified the lack of practical experience and career guidance as major challenges.
Nandita Rani Pal, a student at Daffodil International University; Md Zubayer Ahmed, president of Udarata Youth Foundation; and Ahmad Saeed, founder of Changemakers United, expressed similar concerns.
They said digital skills, English proficiency, information technology, artificial intelligence and practical work experience are becoming increasingly important in the labor market alongside academic qualifications.
Gap between education and employment
Sadia Tabassum, a student at Begum Badrunnesa Government Girls’ College, said many students spend years pursuing education without gaining sufficient understanding of workplace realities.
Md Abdullah Al Mamun Khan, chief executive officer of IVDS Foundation, and Dhruva Chowdhury, a volunteer at OAB Foundation, stressed the need for more hands-on learning, internships, apprenticeships and job-oriented training.
They also called for stronger links between educational institutions and industries so students can gain practical experience alongside their studies.
Mental stress: A silent crisis
The survey also highlighted growing concerns about the mental well-being of young people.
Saleha K, a member of Disable Welfare Society Bangladesh, identified rising frustration and depression among young people as major concerns.
Rabiul Islam, organizing secretary of Gabura Welfare Society, said uncertainty about the future, lack of confidence and inadequate guidance are making many young people increasingly vulnerable to mental stress.
Sanjida Sumiya Suchona, a representative of Geo Avengers, said many young people are becoming frustrated because even after years of education and skills development, they cannot be assured of desired jobs, financial stability or a better quality of life.
She also identified global economic uncertainty, inflation, the climate crisis, political instability and wars as additional sources of pressure.
Digital addiction, online gambling raise concern
Respondents also expressed concern about excessive use of digital technology, online gambling and casino games.
Md Shariful Islam Abhi, founder and director of Islamic Society Sangha Burimari, highlighted mobile phone misuse and drug addiction among young people.
Ayesha Khatun Asha, community facilitator at Youth for Change, said excessive mobile phone use is contributing to reduced attention, wasted time and growing social isolation.
Md Golam Momin, a student at Jatiya Kabi Kazi Nazrul Islam University, identified online gambling and betting as growing threats.
He said the lure of making quick money is pushing many young people toward risky activities.
Reading and social engagement declining
Md Riaz-ul Islam, a volunteer at OAB Foundation, highlighted declining interest in reading among young people.
He said reading is important not only for increasing knowledge but also for developing critical thinking, creativity and values.
Several respondents also said young people’s participation in social and volunteer activities is declining.
Such activities, they noted, can help develop leadership, teamwork and a sense of social responsibility.
Lack of direction and fear of failure
Iti, a program officer at Ancora, said many young people struggle to make decisions based on their potential and abilities because they lack clear goals.
Adel Hossain, general secretary of Independent Blood Bank, said many young people hesitate to start something new because they fear failure. Some also lose interest soon after starting, he added.
He stressed the importance of patience and consistency in developing skills and achieving success.
Youth participation in decision-making remains limited
Jaki Mujahidul Islam, founder and executive director of Fridays for Rights, identified the lack of youth empowerment as a fundamental challenge.
Saifullah Bin Rafiq Chowdhury, finance coordinator at Rise Up, said that although various plans and programs are developed for young people, their participation in policymaking and decision-making remains limited.
As a result, many initiatives do not fully reflect the actual needs of young people, he said.
Migration and a ‘transit mindset’
A relatively different concern was raised by Aman Ullah, adviser to Dipanchal Foundation.
He said a “transit mindset” is emerging among many young people, with many viewing Bangladesh as a temporary stop rather than a place where they envision their long-term future.
Increasingly, he said, young people view migration abroad as the primary pathway to success.
This could reduce their long-term engagement in solving local problems, developing communities and pursuing social initiatives.
To address the issue, Aman Ullah proposed a “Local Stake Initiative” to make young people partners in local development projects.
Young people also point to solutions
Survey respondents proposed a range of solutions, including skills-based education, technical and digital training, internships, career counseling, mentorship, entrepreneurship development, accessible financing, mental health support and greater social engagement.
They said an environment needs to be created where education, skills, employment, mental well-being and civic participation complement one another.
Young people, they said, should not be viewed merely as beneficiaries of development but also as partners in driving it.

item.title: Gas crisis: Energy sector suffers from import reliance
item.description:
• Daily gas demand stands at 3.8 billion cubic feet; supply on normal days 2.7 billion cubic feet

  • LNG supplies 1.05 billion cubic feet a day; a newly arrived vessel is yet to be unloaded due to adverse weather conditions

  • Gas shortages have curtailed power generation, with 3,465MW of load-shedding recorded yesterday

More than 65 per cent of the energy consumed in the country has to be imported. Imports also account for 9 per cent of electricity generation capacity.

For nearly three weeks, the supply of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) has been disrupted, leading to an intensified gas shortage. Power supply from imported electricity has reduced as well, resulting in increased power cuts (load-shedding).

Experts say the country's power and energy sector is suffering precisely due to this reliance on imports.

Sources at the Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla) stated that two weeks after LNG supply dropped by half owing to a fire accident, it registered a slight increase last Thursday. However, adverse weather at sea reduced the supply once again from Monday evening, cutting daily gas supply by over 250 million cubic feet.

If marine conditions improve, supply may increase slightly from today, Wednesday, sources added.

Aninda Islam, Minister of State for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, told Prothom Alo on Tuesday morning that an LNG cargo ship is anchored nearby. Due to adverse weather, the LNG could not be transferred to the terminal. The Energy Division is working with all stakeholders to rapidly boost gas supply.

There are two floating terminals in Moheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, for supplying imported LNG. Among them, the terminal owned by US company Excelerate Energy has a capacity of 600 million cubic feet, while local firm Summit’s terminal has a capacity of 500 million cubic feet.

The national demand for gas stands at 3.8 billion cubic feet per day. Under normal circumstances, the situation is managed by supplying up to 2.7 billion cubic feet, of which 1.05 billion cubic feet comes from LNG.

Following a fire accident on 21 July, Excelerate’s terminal was shut down. This led to a drop in gas supply and worsened the crisis. Production across various sectors—ranging from household cooking stoves to industrial factories and power generation—was disrupted. Long queues of vehicles were also seen at filling stations waiting for CNG.

Stakeholders point out that due to import reliance, any global crisis repeatedly disrupts the country’s energy supply. When the Russia-Ukraine war broke out in 2022, the gas crisis worsened nationwide. As energy supplies dropped, power cuts ensued.

On 28 February, US-Israel strikes took place in Iran, and Iran retaliated by targeting US bases across various Middle Eastern countries. Consequently, the government struggled to maintain the supply of fuel oil domestically.

This time, the gas crisis escalated after a terminal was shut down due to fire. Earlier in 2024, a terminal remained non-operational for nearly three and a half months following damage caused by a cyclone. Whenever adverse weather conditions arise at sea, apprehensions over LNG supply re-emerge. Although a new vessel carrying LNG arrived on Monday, it could not offload at the terminal owing to rough seas.

Petrobangla sources mentioned that Excelerate's terminal has two boilers, each with a capacity of 300 million cubic feet. One of them was damaged in the fire. The undamaged boiler resumed supplying gas last Thursday, and work is currently underway to commission the damaged boiler.

According to the Petrobangla source, once the damaged boiler is ready for operational testing, the running boiler will need to be shut down. During that period, gas supply from Excelerate's terminal will come to a complete halt. Gas supply can resume after being suspended for at least 12 hours, after which supply will gradually normalise. Therefore, Petrobangla intends to carry out this work on a holiday when gas demand is lower.

M. Shamsul Alam, Energy Adviser, CABThe nation became import-dependent far too early. Had that not happened, such a severe crisis might have been avoided today. However, financial strain could have been mitigated by curbing corruption and plunder. Moreover, proper import management could have averted the crisis.

Two officials from the Energy Division and Petrobangla stated that Excelerate Energy has been asked to submit an action plan regarding the inspection, testing, and supply restoration. Further decisions will be taken after consulting with the Energy Division. Gas supply from Excelerate will not increase any further this week.

Severe shortage in power and gas supply

The national demand for gas stands at 3.8 billion cubic feet per day. Under normal circumstances, the situation is managed by supplying up to 2.7 billion cubic feet, of which 1.05 billion cubic feet comes from LNG.

Following the shutdown of Excelerate’s terminal, Summit’s terminal supplied LNG beyond its capacity for four consecutive days—supplying up to nearly 570 million cubic feet per day during that period. Since then, it has been supplying 500 million cubic feet daily. However, failing to offload LNG from the new ship, Summit reduced supply after 7:00 pm on Monday.

Sources in gas distribution state utilities said Summit was supplying 200 million cubic feet on Tuesday evening, while Excelerate Energy was supplying 300 million cubic feet. Domestic gas fields contributed around 1.63 billion cubic feet.

In total, gas supply stood at around 2.13 billion cubic feet—the lowest level in the past three weeks. Gas distribution companies are struggling to meet demand. If LNG cannot be offloaded from the new ship today, Wednesday, gas supply will fall even further.

Iqbal Hassan Mahmood, Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, stated that the government is working towards a long-term solution to the energy crisis.

Speaking on Tuesday at a seminar titled "Energy Sector Crisis: Prospects and Ways Forward", he remarked that the previous Awami League government did not ensure sustainable development. Consequently, the closure of a single LNG terminal has triggered a countrywide gas outcry.

He added that the incumbent government inherited this crisis in the power and energy sector and is actively managing it.

Speaking at the same seminar on Tuesday afternoon, Minister of State for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam noted a significant gap between electricity demand and supply, as well as in the energy sector.

He affirmed that the government is striving to alleviate public hardship stemming from the energy crisis.

Power cuts persist amid heat

Power cuts did not ease yesterday as electricity generation could not be increased. Data from the Power Development Board (PDB) and Power Grid Bangladesh PLC (PGCB) indicate that highest daily power load-shedding has exceeded 3,000 megawatts over the past few days.

According to the PDB, on Sunday, peak load-shedding reached 3,671 megawatts. It rose to 3,757 megawatts on Monday, before dropping slightly following heavy evening rains. However, it began rising again from Tuesday afternoon, reaching a peak of 3,465 megawatts at 3:00 pm.

PDB officials mentioned that electricity demand rises as temperatures climb, but generation cannot keep pace with demand. Gas shortages have cut power production by nearly 1,500 megawatts. Two major coal-fired power plants are operating below capacity.

The officials further said that caution was being exercised regarding increasing generation from oil-fired power plants due to high costs, as running oil-based plants extensively would increase PDB's financial losses. Petrobangla has been requested to increase gas supply, while coal-fired plants have been directed to maximise production.

Power Division sources stated that coal imports were affected due to outstanding bills owed to power plants, leading to coal shortages at two plants. Adani’s power plant in Jharkhand, India, reduced production on 7 August. Coal supply was disrupted by storms and heavy rain, preventing the plant from maintaining generation levels, though production is expected to increase today.

Experts observe that the previous Awami League government did not prioritise domestic gas exploration and production, leading to a continuous decline in local gas output. LNG imports began in 2018, while electricity imports started in 2013.

According to them, there is no immediate fix for the current energy crisis; imports remain necessary in the short term, but domestic energy sources must be expanded alongside. The current government has placed emphasis on domestic gas exploration, inviting tenders for offshore oil and gas exploration, while initiatives have also been undertaken to boost renewable energy generation.

M. Shamsul Alam, Energy Adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told Prothom Alo that the nation became import-dependent far too early. Had that not happened, such a severe crisis might have been avoided today.

However, financial strain, he said, could have been mitigated by curbing corruption and plunder. Moreover, proper import management could have averted the crisis.

He emphasised the need for cost-effective energy usage aligned with national revenue, warning that generating power from fuel oil instead of importing coal will inevitably drive costs up.

item.title: US helicopter fired on ship that tried to break Iran ports blockade
item.description:
PANAMA-CANAL-TRANSPORT

A US helicopter fired missiles on Tuesday into the engine room of a Panama-flagged cargo ship that attempted to break the American blockade of Iran's ports, the United States military said.

The US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired on and disabled the M/V Vela Nova "after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings from American forces," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on X, adding that the vessel "is no longer transiting to Iran in violation of the US blockade."

It was the third time the United States, in a months-long war against Iran, has forcibly halted a vessel since reinstating the ports blockade on 14 July.

CENTCOM said it has redirected 55 ships that tried to run the blockade and boarded two others as of Tuesday.

US forces previously blockaded Iranian ports from 13 April to 18 June, during which they disabled nine ships and redirected more than 140, according to CENTCOM.

Iran has demanded that the United States end the ports blockade as part of its conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key conduit for oil and gas shipments before the war that has seen traffic plummet due to Tehran's attacks on ships in the area.

US President Donald Trump repeated his frequent claim Tuesday that the United States has taken over the waterway.

"We have total control over the Hormuz Strait right now. They don't have control. We have total control. We own it," Trump told reporters.

item.title: Pakistan interior minister in Iran to discuss regional security
item.description:
Pakistan’s interior minister is visiting Iran to discuss regional security, stability and other developments, the Pakistani foreign office said Wednesday, as Islamabad tries to mediate a resolution to the Middle East war.
Mohsin Naqvi, previously involved in mediation efforts between Iran and the US, is known to be close to the powerful head of the Pakistani army, Asim Munir.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported late Tuesday that Naqvi met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni.
“He is discussing bilateral relations, security, regional security and stability, and constructive engagement amongst the parties in the region and regional developments,” Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman Tahir Andrabi told reporters in Islamabad.
The Iranian government’s website said Naqvi conveyed to Pezeshkian “a message from the Pakistani prime minister and the chief of the army,” without specifying its content.
Tehran insists on retaining control of the Strait of Hormuz after the war and wants to charge fees for passage, repeatedly striking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route. The US has imposed a rival blockade on Iranian ports.
Attacks in the waterway, which was free to transit before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have urged both sides to return to the terms of a subsequent June memorandum that set out a path for peace talks.
Last week Iran said it had agreed a route with neighboring Oman for ships transiting the strait and was finalizing arrangements for jointly managing the strategic waterway.
On Tuesday the US military announced that it had fired on a Panama-flagged cargo ship that attempted to break the American blockade of Iran’s ports.

item.description:
The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase (CCGP) on Wednesday approved procurement of eight cargoes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) through direct international purchases to meet the country’s urgent gas demand amid the volatile geopolitical situation arising from the Iran and US-Israel conflict.
Of the eight cargoes, four will be purchased from two international suppliers.
The committee recommended procuring two cargoes from Blackcube International Ltd, UK at US$15.50 per MMBtu and another two cargoes from Maxwell International SPC, Oman at JKM plus US$0.54 per MMBtu.
The proposals were placed by the Energy and Mineral Resources Division.
The CCGP also recommended the purchase of two LNG cargoes from Zhenyu Shipping Co. Limited, Hong Kong, through the direct procurement process in 2026 at US$14.95 per MMBtu.
In another decision, the committee recommended a long-term government-to-government (G2G) purchase arrangement with Gunvor USA LLC for a total of 117 LNG cargoes between 2026 and 2038.
Under the proposed arrangement, five cargoes will be purchased in 2026, six in 2027 and three in 2028 at a price of JKM plus US$0.0875 per MMBtu.
In addition, three cargoes will be purchased in 2028 and 10 cargoes annually from 2029 to 2038 at a price formula of 121% HH plus US$5.20 per MMBtu.
The LNG procurement decisions come as Bangladesh faces persistent pressure on domestic gas supplies and growing dependence on imported LNG to meet demand from power plants, industries and other consumers.
The government has been increasing spot and direct LNG purchases alongside long-term arrangements to ensure uninterrupted gas supply amid heightened uncertainty in the international energy market.

The approval came at a meeting held at the Bangladesh Secretariat with Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury in the chair.
Under one of the approved proposals, Bangladesh will import 100,000 tonnes of non-basmati parboiled rice from Vietnam under a government-to-government (G2G) arrangement.

PT Trinity Cahya Energy of Indonesia was recommended as the supplier at a total cost of Tk157.86 crore, with the price fixed at $514 per tonne.
Another proposal from the commerce ministry to procure 2 crore litres of refined soybean oil through international open tendering was also approved.
PT Trinity Cahya Energy will supply the soybean oil at a total cost of Tk282.56 crore, with the price fixed at $1.15 per litre.
The committee further approved the procurement of 10,000 tonnes of lentils in 50-kg bags through national open tendering.
Nabil Naba Foods Ltd of Rajshahi was recommended as the supplier at a cost of Tk78.96 crore, with the price fixed at Tk78.96 per kg.

Government plans 100,000 health jobs, prioritizes women
item.description:
The government plans to create and fill 100,000 new positions in the health sector, with women to receive priority for 80,000 of the posts, Mahdi Amin, adviser to the prime minister and spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, said Wednesday.
He made the announcement during the second session of a national conference on implementing the Five-Year Strategic Framework for Achieving the SDGs at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka.
Mahdi also announced plans to gradually introduce employment exchanges across the country to directly connect local employers with job seekers, with disadvantaged and marginalized communities receiving priority.
The employment exchanges will initially be introduced at the divisional level before being expanded to every district, he said.
The initiative will operate through online and offline platforms and provide skills development, capacity building and referral services. The private sector will also be involved in strengthening institutional skills and qualifications, he added.
Mahdi Amin said the government was working to ensure that no citizen was left behind in the country’s development efforts.
“The government is prioritizing the integration of disadvantaged communities into the mainstream economy and social protection system,” he said.
He said efforts were also underway to reduce inequality by increasing domestic and foreign investment, creating jobs, and reforming the education and health sectors.
Mahdi Amin said implementation of the government’s Family Card program began immediately after the election.
The program aims to promote women’s self-reliance and empowerment within families, he said.
A Krishak Card (Farmer Card) will also be introduced for marginalized farmers, providing them with technology-based services and direct access to weather forecasts.
The government is also considering waiving up to Tk10,000 in outstanding loans and interest for farmers, he said.
Government development programs would continue to prioritize young people and women, he added.
Mahdi Amin said the education system would place greater emphasis on practical skills and social values alongside academic qualifications.
The government plans to gradually introduce midday meals and standardized uniforms in primary and secondary schools.
Measures would also be taken to reduce the digital divide by extending the benefits of multimedia classrooms in urban schools to rural institutions.
He stressed the importance of teacher training and enhancing the dignity and status of teachers.
On the energy sector, Mahdi Amin said it was facing major challenges due to long-standing administrative and infrastructural problems.
A temporary gas supply crisis had emerged after a floating LNG terminal became technically inoperable, but measures were being taken to resolve the issue, he said.
The government is also working to attract foreign investment in the energy sector while taking initiatives to extract domestic natural resources, he added.
Efforts are underway to find a sustainable medium-term solution, he said.
The government had also sought to provide relief to ordinary people by reducing taxes and VAT on several essential commodities and keeping fuel prices under control.
Mahdi Amin also emphasized ensuring workers receive their salaries, bonuses and other financial benefits.
The conference discussed strategies for inclusive development, reforms and implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals during July 2026–June 2031.
Speakers said ensuring marginalized people’s access to government services, strengthening administrative accountability and reducing inequality would be crucial to sustainable development.
Social Welfare Minister Professor Dr AZM Zahid Hossain said Bangladesh currently ranks 110th in SDG implementation.
With less than five years remaining to achieve the goals, he stressed the need for accelerated progress.
He said the government was working to build a Bangladesh for everyone.
Mahdi Amin said initiatives such as tree plantation, canal excavation and water-resource management would be undertaken to reduce disparities in facilities and opportunities between urban and rural areas.
The government’s goal is to ensure equal rights and participation in development for all citizens, regardless of political opinion, religion, race, physical ability or geographical location, he said.
The three-day conference was organized by the General Economics Division of the Bangladesh Planning Commission and the Governance Innovation Unit of the Prime Minister’s Office, with the participation of the Citizen’s Platform.
CPD Distinguished Fellow Debapriya Bhattacharya, BNP Standing Committee member Selima Rahman, Member of Parliament Madhabi Marmas, and representatives and stakeholders from various levels attended the conference.

item.title: When seasons lose their rhythm: Bangladesh’s new climatic reality
item.description:
Only two months ago, Bangladesh was experiencing one of the hottest periods of the year. Heatwaves swept across many districts, and people were advised to stay indoors. Driven by changing global climate systems, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) had predicted an intense dry period for this year. Ten more heatwaves were predicted to occur between June and August.

While the BMD later flagged standard early-July warnings of heavy rainfall due to a monsoon depression, few could have anticipated the sheer violence of the downpour. What followed was a period of torrential, July brought days of torrential rainfall that swelled rivers, inundated roads, and plunged major parts of the country into severe flooding and waterlogging, leaving people completely unprepared for the devastation.

For many people, this raised an obvious question: What is happening to our weather?

Some may see these events as isolated incidents, but they are part of a much larger pattern. Climate change is not only increasing temperatures; it is making weather patterns increasingly irregular. Bangladesh is gradually moving from a climate where seasons followed a familiar rhythm to one where weather is becoming much harder to anticipate.

A few decades ago, life in Bangladesh followed a seasonal calendar that people understood well. Farmers prepared their land knowing roughly when the monsoon would arrive. Aman rice was transplanted according to expected rainfall, while wheat, mustard, potatoes and vegetables were planted after winter set in. Fishermen understood seasonal river conditions, and even many social and cultural activities were organised around predictable weather patterns.

Of course, weather was never perfectly consistent. There were floods, droughts and cyclones. But these were exceptions rather than the norm. Most years, people could rely on the general timing of the seasons. Their knowledge came from experience built over generations.

Today, that confidence is gradually disappearing.

Bangladesh is particularly vulnerable because its economy and livelihoods are closely tied to seasonal weather. Agriculture still employs millions of people, and crop production depends heavily on the timing of rainfall and temperature.

Rain often arrives later than expected, or sometimes much earlier. Heavy rainfall may occur within just a few days instead of being distributed across several weeks. Winters are becoming shorter and warmer. Heatwaves are arriving earlier and lasting longer. Instead of one predictable seasonal cycle, Bangladesh is increasingly experiencing sudden shifts between prolonged dry conditions and intense rainfall.

The recent heavy rainfall in July illustrates this change. After months of extreme heat, many people welcomed the rain, expecting relief from the scorching temperatures. Yet the rainfall was so intense that it caused flooding and waterlogging in many places. This shows that the challenge is no longer simply whether it rains, but when, how much, and how quickly the rain falls.

Why is this happening?

The underlying cause lies in how climate change affects the Earth's atmosphere. On a global scale, scientists attribute this phenomenon to the intensification of the hydrological cycle caused by global warming. As greenhouse gas emissions continue to warm the planet, the atmosphere becomes warmer and capable of holding more moisture. This changes the entire water cycle. More water evaporates from rivers, ponds, wetlands and the soil. As a result, rainfall is becoming more concentrated, with intense downpours occurring over a short period and longer dry spells in between.

Data from the BMD reveals that the country’s traditional monsoon schedule is actively shifting. June, which traditionally marks the arrival of steady monsoon rains, has increasingly recorded below-average rainfall; nearly 30 per cent less than normal this year. Combined with persistently high temperatures, these dry conditions allowed heat to build up. When rain finally arrived in July, much of the seasonal rainfall fell within a short period, leading to flooding and waterlogging in many parts of the country.

Bangladesh is particularly vulnerable because its economy and livelihoods are closely tied to seasonal weather. Agriculture still employs millions of people, and crop production depends heavily on the timing of rainfall and temperature. When seasons become irregular, farming becomes much more difficult.

For instance, in northwestern Bangladesh, one of the country's drought-prone regions, many people no longer trust the traditional agricultural calendar. They know that summers are becoming hotter, but their greatest concern is uncertainty. Rain sometimes arrives too late for cultivation. At other times, heavy rainfall damages crops just before harvest.

Heatwaves dry out the soil rapidly, increasing irrigation needs, while sudden downpours often fail to compensate for the earlier moisture loss because much of the water runs off quickly instead of replenishing the soil and groundwater. These sufferings are also experienced by farmers in coastal areas, and floodplains. Although the challenges differ from one region to another, the underlying problem is the same: weather patterns are becoming less reliable.

This growing unpredictability has consequences beyond agriculture. It affects water management, fisheries, transport, public health and even household finances. When heavy rainfall occurs unexpectedly, cities experience waterlogging because drainage systems cannot cope with such intense rainfall. When heatwaves become longer, electricity demand rises while outdoor workers face greater health risks. Every sector is forced to deal with greater uncertainty.

Perhaps the biggest challenge is that Bangladesh's climate policies still tend to treat floods, droughts and heatwaves as separate problems. In reality, they are increasingly connected. A prolonged heatwave can dry out the soil, followed by intense rainfall that causes flooding instead of slowly replenishing water resources. One climate extreme often creates the conditions for another.

This means that adaptation strategies must also change. Bangladesh certainly needs stronger embankments, better drainage systems and improved irrigation. However, it also needs better seasonal forecasting, climate information services for farmers, improved groundwater management, crop insurance and stronger local planning that recognises increasing climate variability.

Climate change is often described as a problem of rising temperatures. That description is no longer enough. The greater challenge facing Bangladesh today is the growing unpredictability of its weather. It is not simply that summers are hotter or rainfall is heavier. It is that the natural rhythm on which people have depended for generations is gradually breaking down.

The recent July rainfall should therefore not be seen as an isolated weather event. It is another reminder that Bangladesh is entering a new climatic reality. Learning to live with this reality will require more than disaster response. It will require rethinking how we plan our agriculture, manage our water resources and prepare our communities for a future where uncertainty itself has become one of the greatest consequences of climate change.

* Ummey Kulsum is a lecturer at the Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Rajshahi.

item.title: Turkey backs Saudi-led maritime defence coalition in Red Sea
item.description:
Turkey backs Saudi-led maritime defence coalition in Red Sea

Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 10:37
The move would help deepen the trilateral defence pact between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan
Turkish Navy helicopters and ships on military exercises in the Mediterranean Sea near Antalya on 9 April (AFP/Adem Altan)
Off

Turkey confirmed on Thursday for the first time that it had joined efforts to establish a multinational maritime defence coalition aimed at ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea.

The announcement signals increased cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Ankara after the signing of a trilateral pact between the states and Pakistan in Mecca last week.

“At the invitation of Saudi Arabia, a technical meeting was held in Riyadh on 28 July to ensure freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, followed by a meeting of the chiefs of general staff on 30 July 2026,” the Turkish Ministry of National Defence said in a statement.

The ministry added that Turkey was participating in another coordination meeting on the establishment of the maritime defence coalition in Jeddah on Thursday.

“Work continues with the Saudi Arabian authorities to reduce tensions in the Gulf region and ensure the uninterrupted flow of international trade,” the statement said.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a defence pact last week committing the three countries to each other’s security, including collective security obligations.

Several Ankara-based sources who spoke to Middle East Eye said they believed the Red Sea coalition would be the first area in which the alliance between Turkey and Saudi Arabia would deepen.

Saudi Arabia announced last month that it had established a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea.

The move followed the Houthis’ declaration on 20 July that they had imposed a maritime blockade on the kingdom, disrupting oil shipments diverted to the Red Sea following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The alliance reportedly includes Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar,  Somalia and Yemen.

It will be headquartered in Riyadh.
