Gas shortage deepens Bangladesh power crisis, load-shedding hits 3,592MW
item.description:
Sweltering heat and prolonged power cuts are disrupting daily life across Bangladesh, with some rural areas facing 10-12 hours of load-shedding a day.
The outages are disrupting agriculture, small businesses, grocery shops, workshops and online work, while students and employees are struggling to work and study. Children, elderly people and the ill are suffering the most, particularly during nighttime outages.
The crisis is mainly being blamed on a shortage of fuel, particularly natural gas. Several gas-fired power plants cannot operate at full capacity due to inadequate gas supplies, leaving the country unable to fully utilize its installed generation capacity.
Rising electricity demand amid the heat has further widened the supply gap.
The shortfall was particularly severe between August 11 and 12. Load-shedding peaked at 3,592MW at midnight on August 11, when demand was 17,523MW against a supply of 13,931MW.
Demand peaked at 18,043MW at 9pm, with supply at 15,036MW and a deficit of 3,007MW. The shortfall remained above 3,000MW at 1am and 2am on August 12.
Although the situation improved somewhat in the morning, load-shedding rose again to 2,688MW at noon and 3,382MW at 3pm.
Power supply is generally stable from December to March, when demand remains relatively low. But load-shedding typically begins as temperatures rise in April, increases in May and June, eases somewhat in July and rises again in August.
Demand that stood at just over 9,000MW during peak hours at the beginning of the year surged to 18,043MW on August 11.
Besides inadequate gas supplies, declining domestic gas production and pressure on coal and liquid fuel supplies and costs have worsened the crisis.
Most gas-fired plants are operating below capacity. Officials expect generation to increase once the Maheshkhali terminal resumes normal gas supplies.
Rural areas are facing the longest outages, with electricity unavailable for up to 10-12 hours in many places.
The crisis is also affecting agriculture, small businesses, grocery shops, workshops and online-based work. Problems with mobile networks and internet services in some areas are creating additional difficulties for students and employees.
Nighttime outages are also raising security concerns. Frustrated residents have attacked rural electricity facilities in some areas.
The Bangladesh Palli Bidyut Association on Wednesday sought enhanced security from the inspector general of police (IGP) for grids, substations and offices following reports of attacks, vandalism and arson.
In a letter to the IGP, the association said around 80 rural electricity cooperatives provide power to nearly 40 million customers across the country, with a significant share of the country’s electricity distributed through them.
However, as power generation continues to fall short of demand, the cooperatives are being forced to impose prolonged load-shedding.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit said the shortage was caused by disruptions to gas-fired generation and said the situation would improve somewhat from Wednesday evening.
However, he said no specific timeline could be given for fully resolving the fuel crisis.
PGCB data showed load-shedding at 1,319MW at 6pm on August 12, down from 2,499MW at the same time the previous day.
Officials said the evening improvement was partly because oil-fired plants were brought online during peak hours, while outages increase again after those plants are shut down at night.
‘We operate with whatever allocation we receive’
West Zone Power distribution Company Executive Director Mohammad Rokonuzzaman said the company serves around 1.8 million customers in 21 district towns and 22 upazila towns.
“Demand is around 700MW. Load-shedding was around 100MW. Yesterday (Tuesday), it was around 140-150MW,” he said.
He said the company was managing the situation with three to four hours of daily load-shedding and had sought government security amid growing public anger.
Energy expert BD Rahmat Ullah said the fuel crisis could not be resolved immediately and warned that the power shortage would continue until the fuel shortage eases.
He recommended greater investment in renewable energy, particularly rooftop solar, to prevent similar crises in the future.

Teesta master plan work to begin next year
item.description:
The main implementation work on the Teesta Master Plan will begin next year, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Water Resources was informed on Thursday.
The committee held its first meeting at the National parliament Bhaban, with Chairman of the committee Mohammad Shafiqul Haque Milon, MP, in the chair. The meeting began with an introductory session, followed by a review of the Water Resources Ministry’s activities over the past six months. Members noted significant progress in several areas of the ministry’s work.
The meeting discussed advance measures to prevent river erosion, tree plantation and other initiatives. It was also informed that the Padma Barrage Project had received approval from the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC). The committee was further briefed on strong assurances regarding the renewal of the Farakka Treaty.
A presentation on the ministry’s overall activities was made at the meeting, covering ongoing development projects, progress, implementation timelines and budget allocations.
The ministry currently has 93 development projects under implementation, with Tk 7,832.80 crore allocated for them in the 2026-27 fiscal year, the meeting was told.
The committee urged the ministry to complete projects within their stipulated deadlines, ensure the proper and efficient use of allocated funds and take more effective measures to improve public services.
Water Resources Minister Mohammad Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee, State Minister Farhad Hossain Azad, and committee members AKM Fazlul Haque Milon, AE Sultan Mahmud Babu, Alamgir Mohammad Mahfuz Ullah Farid, Munsi Rafiqul Alam, Md Izzat Ullah, Md Mashiur Rahman Khan and Md Oli Ullah attended the meeting.
The Water Resources Ministry secretary, directors general of various agencies under the ministry, senior officials, heads of relevant agencies and officials from the Jatiya Sangsad Secretariat were also present.

Global youth unemployment rises to 12.4pc amid weak job creation: ILO
item.description:
Global youth unemployment rose to 12.4 per cent in 2025, with 67 million young people aged 15 to 24 unemployed, as sluggish economic growth and weak job creation made it harder for young people to enter the labour market, according to a new International Labour Organisation (ILO) report.

The ILO’s ‘Global Employment Trends for Youth 2026: Back to the Future’ report also found that the share of young people not in employment, education or training (NEET) increased slightly to 20 per cent, affecting more than 257 million people.

Between 2023 and 2025, youth unemployment increased in eight of the world’s 11 subregions, driven by slowing economic growth, weak job creation, geopolitical tensions and rapid technological change, the report said.

Job prospects worsen in higher-income economies

Some of the sharpest increases were recorded in higher-income economies. In Northern America, youth unemployment rose from 8.3 per cent in 2023 to 9.8 per cent in 2025. In Northern, Southern and Western Europe, it remained high at 15 per cent.

The decline in middle-skilled jobs has made it harder for young people to establish stable careers, the report said. Clerical and administrative positions, service and sales jobs, manufacturing-related occupations and some technical roles, which have traditionally served as entry points for young workers, are shrinking.

Shortage of decent jobs in developing economies

In developing economies, the key challenge remains creating enough decent jobs to absorb growing young populations. Low unemployment rates in these countries often mask widespread insecurity, as many young people cannot afford to remain unemployed and instead enter informal or unstable work.

Nearly nine in 10 young workers aged 15 to 29 in low- and lower-middle-income countries are employed informally, limiting their access to stable incomes and social protection.

Sub-Saharan Africa faces particularly strong demographic pressures alongside insufficient decent jobs, resulting in more young people falling into NEET status, the report said.

The Arab States and Northern Africa recorded the world’s highest youth unemployment rates in 2025, at 26.2 per cent and 22.6 per cent respectively. In both regions, at least one in three young people were NEET.

AI reshaping youth employment

Technological change including advances in artificial intelligence is also transforming employment opportunities for young people.

According to the report, 6.1 per cent of jobs held by people aged 15 to 29 are in occupations highly exposed to AI-related changes. Many of these are among middle-skilled occupations that have declined since 2023, particularly clerical and administrative roles.

At the same time, demand is growing for some knowledge-based technical occupations in science, health and engineering, highlighting the need for young people to acquire skills suited to changing labour markets.

“There is increasing noise around AI,” said Sukti Dasgupta, ILO director of the Employment, Skills and Sustainable Enterprises Department. She said governments should increase investment in skills, lifelong learning and social protection so young people can adapt to technological changes.

ILO Director-General Gilbert F. Houngbo said young people unable to find decent work cannot build their futures with confidence.

“When young people are locked out of quality employment, countries lose talent, productivity and social cohesion,” he said, adding that creating decent jobs for young people is both a social imperative and a smart investment.

The report calls for greater investment in quality education, lifelong learning and apprenticeships, stronger employment services, expanded social protection and policies to create more decent jobs.

It also recommends a human-centred approach to AI governance so that technological innovation creates opportunities rather than deepening inequality.

item.title: Bomb trail raises spectre of militant regrouping
item.description:
A string of bomb recoveries and explosions around Savar and Ashulia has raised fresh concerns over possible militant regrouping on Dhaka’s doorstep, with investigators linking some recent incidents to suspected Neo-JMB operatives and warning of plans for major acts of sabotage.
At least 16 explosives, including two powerful pressure cooker-type bombs, have been recovered from Savar and Ashulia over the past two weeks.
The latest discoveries came on Tuesday, when police recovered 14 pipe bombs and bomb-making materials in separate operations and found another powerful device near a madrasa and mosque in Savar.
The developments are part of a wider pattern emerging since late last year.
Investigators believe members of Neo-JMB may have links to at least 11 incidents since an explosion at Al-Qura Madrasa in South Keraniganj on December 26, including bomb attacks, weapons recoveries and explosives found in Dhaka and surrounding districts.
Police have stepped up intelligence surveillance, patrols and searches, but several questions remain unanswered -- particularly over who is producing the explosives, where the materials are coming from and whether the incidents are part of a coordinated attempt to reorganise militant networks.
The latest alarm came on August 11 when a pressure cooker-type bomb wrapped in black tape was discovered in a forested area in front of Jamia Ilmul Ilah Society Madrasa and Jame Masjid at Laltek Goper Bari in Savar.
The DMP bomb disposal unit later defused the device.
The same night, police recovered nine explosives and bomb-making equipment from a house in Shyampur after arresting Arif Hossain in Hemayetpur with five explosives.
Police said a total of 14 pipe bombs were recovered during the operation.
A similar pressure cooker-type bomb had been recovered from a travel bag outside a grocery store in Ashulia on July 30.
Earlier, on July 11, 20-year-old Rony suffered severe injuries, including damage to his wrist and four fingers, when an explosive went off while he was allegedly making a cocktail inside a room in Ashulia.
Five days earlier, an explosion at an NCP rally in Savar left at least four people injured.
Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parveen said intelligence had indicated that suspected militants were operating in the area and had prepared two particularly destructive bombs.
She said: “We had some information. We came to know that militants might be staying here. As you know, those who were involved in the Keraniganj madrasa incident came from there and took shelter with us here.”
She said: “We had information that they had made two big and destructive bombs. We were able to recover both of them.”
Police have increased intelligence surveillance through the Detective Branch and District Special Branch, alongside patrols and searches. Residents, particularly landlords in densely populated workers’ neighbourhoods, have also been asked to verify tenants.
Investigators have drawn connections between the recent Savar operations and the December explosion at the Keraniganj madrasa.
Following that blast, investigators recovered a mobile phone that led to a February raid in Jessore, where 10 powerful grenades, three foreign pistols, ammunition and sharp weapons were recovered.
Investigators are also examining suspected links to an attack on police in Kutubkhali in February, a bomb attack on a temple in Comilla in March, the killing of a minority community member in Feni, a pipe-bomb explosion in Jatrabari, an attack on intelligence officials in Uttara and the recovery of a bomb beneath Motijheel Metrorail station.
Police alleged in a case filed under the Anti-Terrorism Act that those involved in the latest Savar operation were members of Neo-JMB who had gathered with explosives to carry out subversive activities.
Arif has been arrested, while several other accused remain absconding.
Savar and Ashulia’s enormous population, industrial neighbourhoods and constantly changing population make the area particularly difficult to monitor, according to police and crime experts.
SP Shamima Parveen said: “This area is densely populated. Workers live here and they are mostly floating. There is a situation here where they come today and are not there tomorrow.”
She said these characteristics could make the area attractive to people seeking to conceal their identities or activities.
Crime expert Dr Touhidul Haque of Dhaka University said: “Areas around Dhaka like Savar, Narayanganj and Gazipur have become a kind of shelter for criminals. They choose these areas because it is relatively easy to live with little money and mix with locals and make bomb cocktails. Criminals are also brought here from other places and kept here.”
He called for stronger intelligence gathering, tenant verification and monitoring of the sale and purchase of materials that can be used in explosives.
Human rights activist Nur Khan Liton cautioned against prematurely dismissing the recent discoveries as staged, a suspicion shaped partly by controversies surrounding some alleged militant incidents under the previous government.
Nur Khan said: “Since people have seen or suspected many staged dramas in the past, they have a suspicion in this case too. But as much as there was reason to suspect in the context of that time, there is less reason to suspect in today’s context.”
He said: “No thought or ideology actually dies. It can be temporarily stagnant for various reasons.”
His assessment is that extremist elements may be attempting to reorganise, potentially recruiting supporters and seeking training opportunities.
Savar’s association with militant activity is not new.
During JMB’s coordinated nationwide bombings on August 17, 2005, six bombs exploded in Savar.
Ten-year-old Abdus Salam was killed and another child was injured. JMB later claimed responsibility for the nationwide attacks.
In 2010, RAB arrested three suspected militants, including the then head of JMB’s Dhaka division, from Savar and recovered petrol bombs and bomb-making materials.
Seven years later, RAB arrested three members of the JMB-linked Sarwar-Tamim group in Savar with firearms, plastic explosives and bomb-making materials.
Months later, four suspected members of the same group surrendered after security forces surrounded an alleged militant hideout in Ashulia.
They had reportedly rented the property posing as garment workers.
Nearly two decades after JMB’s nationwide bombing campaign first exposed Savar’s militant footprint, the latest trail of explosives has brought the area back under scrutiny.
This time, investigators face a more immediate question: whether the bombs being recovered are remnants of scattered extremist activity, or signs that an organised network is again taking shape on the outskirts of the capital.
